lesson.title: Facts, opinions and theories: entrepreneurial thinking

learning_objectives.en: Distinguish checkable facts from personal opinions and tentative predictions.
learning_objectives.vi: Phân biệt dữ kiện kiểm chứng được, quan điểm chủ quan và dự đoán chưa xác thực.

content.en: A fact can in principle be checked with evidence; an opinion expresses a judgment; a theory or prediction proposes an explanation or future outcome that still requires testing. Signal words can help, but verify the purpose of the whole sentence.
content.vi: Fact có thể kiểm tra bằng chứng; opinion thể hiện đánh giá; theory/prediction nêu giải thích hay dự đoán cần kiểm chứng. Từ khóa giúp định hướng, nhưng phải xét nghĩa cả câu.

example.en: The company employed six people (fact); its service is excellent (opinion); the firm might expand (prediction).
example.vi: Công ty có sáu nhân viên (dữ kiện); dịch vụ xuất sắc (ý kiến); có thể mở rộng (dự đoán).

vocabulary.example_vi: Tiền thuê cao hơn làm giảm biên lợi nhuận.

vocabulary.example_en: She learned how to run a business.
vocabulary.example_vi: Cô học cách điều hành doanh nghiệp.

vocabulary.example_vi: Lịch làm việc linh hoạt có thể cải thiện khả năng giữ chân nhân viên.

strategies.en: Ask whether someone could verify the statement, or whether it expresses evaluation or an uncertain forecast.
strategies.vi: Hỏi xem phát biểu có thể đối chiếu số liệu không, có đánh giá chủ quan hay dự báo chưa chắc chắn không.

common_mistakes.wrong: The company is definitely the best. = Fact
common_mistakes.correct: The company employed six technicians. = Checkable claim

reason.en: Value judgements are not verifiable facts.
reason.vi: Đánh giá “tốt nhất” không phải dữ kiện có thể xác minh.

mini_review.en: Can I explain an answer or response using evidence or a clear reason?
mini_review.vi: Tôi có thể giải thích đáp án/bài nói bằng bằng chứng hoặc lý do rõ không?

mini_review.vi: Tôi có thể áp dụng kỹ năng sang chủ đề mới mà không sao chép mẫu không?

passages.title: Four entrepreneurs, four practical ideas (original profiles)
passages.text:
[A] Maya Chen founded a small repair service after noticing that students often threw away working laptops because a replacement seemed easier than getting help. She started with a borrowed desk, learned to diagnose common faults and offered clear prices before beginning any work. Two years later, the business employed six technicians. Maya argues that reliable service matters more than advertising when customers must trust someone with their devices.

[B] Idris Bello had a different beginning. He worked in a large food factory before building a company that sells affordable, nutritious meals to offices. At first, his team prepared more food than customers ordered, and waste threatened the business. He introduced a simple digital ordering system that allowed clients to choose meals the previous day. The change reduced waste and helped his company become profitable without increasing prices.

[C] Sofia Alvarez grew up in a rural town where many artists struggled to sell their work. She created an online platform that connects local makers with buyers in larger cities. Her team provides photography, packaging and delivery support. Although the website was expensive to build, Sofia believes the greatest success is that young people can earn money without leaving their communities.

[D] Peter Novak took over a family bicycle shop that had operated for thirty years. Competition from internet retailers caused sales to fall, so he began organising maintenance workshops and weekend cycling events. The shop now earns part of its income from repairs and training, not just selling bicycles. Peter still worries about rising rent, but says that a local business can survive by becoming part of the neighbourhood instead of competing only on price.
